items.stem: Which of these metals is magnetic?
items.answer: Nickel
items.markingKey: Iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic; aluminium, copper and brass are not.

items.stem: Explain why an unmagnetised iron nail is attracted to either pole of a magnet.
items.answer: Magnetism is induced in the nail: the end nearest the magnet becomes the opposite pole, so it is always attracted.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: induced magnetism; 1 mark: near end opposite pole → attraction.

items.stem: Explain why repulsion, not attraction, is the only sure test that an object is a magnet.
items.answer: Attraction occurs between a magnet and any magnetic material, so it does not prove the object is a magnet; only a magnet can repel another magnet.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: Elena has three identical-looking bars: one is a magnet, one is soft iron and one is aluminium. Bar B attracts the north pole of a compass; bar D has no effect. Describe further tests to identify all three bars and explain the reasoning.
items.answer: Bar D is aluminium (not magnetic). Test bar B with both compass poles: if one end repels a pole, B is the magnet; if it attracts both poles, it is soft iron and the remaining bar is the magnet.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: non-magnetic identified; 1 mark: repulsion test; 1 mark: correct conclusion logic.

items.stem: Diego has three identical-looking bars: one is a magnet, one is soft iron and one is aluminium. Bar A attracts the north pole of a compass; bar B has no effect. Describe further tests to identify all three bars and explain the reasoning.
items.answer: Bar B is aluminium (not magnetic). Test bar A with both compass poles: if one end repels a pole, A is the magnet; if it attracts both poles, it is soft iron and the remaining bar is the magnet.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: non-magnetic identified; 1 mark: repulsion test; 1 mark: correct conclusion logic.

items.stem: A doorbell uses an electromagnet to make a hammer strike a bell. (a) Describe how to find the shape and direction of the magnetic field around the magnet. (b) Suggest why the device could fail if the coil were wound on a steel core.
items.answer: (a) Place a plotting compass at many points and mark the needle direction; join the marks into lines from N to S. (b) Steel keeps its magnetism, so the object would stay attracted after switching off.

items.stem: What happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the north pole of another?
items.answer: They repel
items.markingKey: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What is meant by induced magnetism? (b) What happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the north pole of another?
items.answer: (a) A magnetic material becoming a magnet when placed in a magnetic field (b) They repel
items.markingKey: (a) Induced magnetism: a magnetic material is magnetised by a nearby magnet; the near end gets the opposite pole. (b) Like poles repel, unlike poles attract.

items.stem: Describe how to demagnetise a steel bar using electricity.
items.answer: Place it in a coil carrying alternating current and slowly pull it out of the coil (or reduce the a.c. to zero).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a.c. coil; 1 mark: withdraw slowly / reduce current.

items.stem: A chain of iron paper clips hangs from a magnet. Explain what happens when the magnet is removed if the clips are soft iron, and if they are steel.
items.answer: Soft iron clips lose their induced magnetism and fall apart; steel clips keep some magnetism and may stay together.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: Explain why scrap-yard cranes use electromagnets rather than permanent magnets.
items.answer: The magnetism can be switched off to drop the load, and its strength can be changed with the current.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: Mei has three identical-looking bars: one is a magnet, one is soft iron and one is aluminium. Bar D attracts the north pole of a compass; bar A has no effect. Describe further tests to identify all three bars and explain the reasoning.
items.answer: Bar A is aluminium (not magnetic). Test bar D with both compass poles: if one end repels a pole, D is the magnet; if it attracts both poles, it is soft iron and the remaining bar is the magnet.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: non-magnetic identified; 1 mark: repulsion test; 1 mark: correct conclusion logic.

items.stem: Priya is designing a simple door lock that uses an electromagnet to hold a steel bolt. (a) Explain why the core should be made of soft iron rather than steel. (b) Suggest why the device could fail if the coil were wound on a steel core.
items.answer: (a) Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily, so the magnet switches off when the current stops. (b) Steel keeps its magnetism, so the object would stay attracted after switching off.

items.stem: A doorbell uses an electromagnet to make a hammer strike a bell. (a) Describe how to find the shape and direction of the magnetic field around the magnet. (b) Explain why aluminium is not attracted. (c) Explain what happens to an iron object touching the magnet when the current is switched off.
items.answer: (a) Place a plotting compass at many points and mark the needle direction; join the marks into lines from N to S. (b) Aluminium is not a magnetic material; no magnetism is induced in it. (c) Its induced magnetism disappears and it is released/falls.

items.stem: A school technician is asked to store some bar magnets and soft-iron rods safely. (a) Explain why the core should be made of soft iron rather than steel. (b) State two ways to make the electromagnet stronger.
items.answer: (a) Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily, so the magnet switches off when the current stops. (b) More turns; larger current (or soft-iron core).

items.stem: Magnetic field lines outside a bar magnet point
options: from the south pole to the north pole
from the north pole to the south pole
items.answer: from the north pole to the south pole
items.markingKey: Direction of the field = direction a free north pole would move: N to S outside the magnet.

items.stem: Explain why magnetic field lines never cross.
items.answer: At any point the field has only one direction; if lines crossed, a compass there would point two ways at once.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: Describe the field between a north pole and a south pole placed close together, facing each other.
items.answer: Fairly uniform: parallel, equally spaced lines from N to S in the gap.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: parallel equally spaced; 1 mark: N → S direction.

items.stem: On a field diagram, point Q has field lines 4 times closer together than point Z. State what this tells you about the field and suggest where each point might be on a bar magnet.
items.answer: The field is stronger where lines are closer; the first point is nearer a pole, the second further away (or near the middle/side).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: closer lines = stronger field; 1 mark: sensible positions.

items.stem: On a field diagram, point X has field lines 3 times closer together than point Z. State what this tells you about the field and suggest where each point might be on a bar magnet.
items.answer: The field is stronger where lines are closer; the first point is nearer a pole, the second further away (or near the middle/side).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: closer lines = stronger field; 1 mark: sensible positions.

items.stem: Kenji wants to compare the strength of two bar magnets using only a plotting compass and a metre rule. Plan an experiment, stating the measurements, control variables and how the result will be decided.
items.answer: Place the compass on a line east–west so the Earth’s field is perpendicular; bring each magnet along the same line until the needle deflects by a fixed angle (e.g. 45°) and measure the distance from the compass. The magnet that does this from further away is stronger. Control: same orientation, same compass, no other magnetic materials nearby; repeat and average.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: measure distance for a fixed deflection (or deflection at fixed distance); 1 mark: control variables (orientation, location away from iron); 1 mark: repeats; 1 mark: conclusion rule.

items.stem: Where is the magnetic field of a bar magnet strongest?
options: In the middle of the magnet
items.answer: At the poles
items.markingKey: Field lines are closest together at the poles.

items.stem: Describe the magnetic field between two north poles placed near each other.
items.answer: Field lines from both poles curve away; there is a neutral point midway where the fields cancel.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lines repel/curve away; 1 mark: neutral point.

items.stem: Explain how iron filings show a magnetic field pattern but do not show its direction.
items.answer: Each filing becomes a tiny induced magnet and lines up with the field, but filings have no marked north end, so the direction is not shown.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.answer: (a) Magnetism is induced in the nail: the end nearest the magnet becomes the opposite pole, so it is always attracted. (b) Attraction occurs between a magnet and any magnetic material, so it does not prove the object is a magnet; only a magnet can repel another magnet.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: induced magnetism; 1 mark: near end opposite pole → attraction. (b) 1 mark each.

items.stem: Omar has three identical-looking bars: one is a magnet, one is soft iron and one is aluminium. Bar C attracts the north pole of a compass; bar D has no effect. Describe further tests to identify all three bars and explain the reasoning.
items.answer: Bar D is aluminium (not magnetic). Test bar C with both compass poles: if one end repels a pole, C is the magnet; if it attracts both poles, it is soft iron and the remaining bar is the magnet.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: non-magnetic identified; 1 mark: repulsion test; 1 mark: correct conclusion logic.

items.stem: A scrap-yard crane uses a large electromagnet to lift old cars. (a) Explain why the core should be made of soft iron rather than steel. (b) Explain why aluminium is not attracted.
items.answer: (a) Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily, so the magnet switches off when the current stops. (b) Aluminium is not a magnetic material; no magnetism is induced in it.

items.stem: A doorbell uses an electromagnet to make a hammer strike a bell. (a) State two ways to make the electromagnet stronger. (b) Describe how to find the shape and direction of the magnetic field around the magnet.
items.answer: (a) More turns; larger current (or soft-iron core). (b) Place a plotting compass at many points and mark the needle direction; join the marks into lines from N to S.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which material is best for making a permanent magnet? (b) What is meant by induced magnetism?
items.answer: (a) Steel (b) A magnetic material becoming a magnet when placed in a magnetic field
items.markingKey: (a) Steel is hard to magnetise but keeps its magnetism. (b) Induced magnetism: a magnetic material is magnetised by a nearby magnet; the near end gets the opposite pole.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why an unmagnetised iron nail is attracted to either pole of a magnet. (b) Explain why scrap-yard cranes use electromagnets rather than permanent magnets.
items.answer: (a) Magnetism is induced in the nail: the end nearest the magnet becomes the opposite pole, so it is always attracted. (b) The magnetism can be switched off to drop the load, and its strength can be changed with the current.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: induced magnetism; 1 mark: near end opposite pole → attraction. (b) 1 mark each.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A chain of iron paper clips hangs from a magnet. Explain what happens when the magnet is removed if the clips are soft iron, and if they are steel. (b) Explain why scrap-yard cranes use electromagnets rather than permanent magnets.
items.answer: (a) Soft iron clips lose their induced magnetism and fall apart; steel clips keep some magnetism and may stay together. (b) The magnetism can be switched off to drop the load, and its strength can be changed with the current.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. (b) 1 mark each.

items.stem: Sipho is designing a simple door lock that uses an electromagnet to hold a steel bolt. Explain why the core should be made of soft iron rather than steel.
items.answer: Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily, so the magnet switches off when the current stops.

items.stem: Sipho is designing a simple door lock that uses an electromagnet to hold a steel bolt. Suggest why the device could fail if the coil were wound on a steel core.
items.answer: Steel keeps its magnetism, so the object would stay attracted after switching off.

items.stem: A scrap-yard crane uses a large electromagnet to lift old cars. (a) Explain why the core should be made of soft iron rather than steel. (b) Explain why aluminium is not attracted. (c) Explain what happens to an iron object touching the magnet when the current is switched off.
items.answer: (a) Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily, so the magnet switches off when the current stops. (b) Aluminium is not a magnetic material; no magnetism is induced in it. (c) Its induced magnetism disappears and it is released/falls.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which apparatus can be used to plot the field lines around a bar magnet? (b) Magnetic field lines outside a bar magnet point
items.answer: (a) A plotting compass (b) from the north pole to the south pole
items.markingKey: (a) Move a small plotting compass and mark the direction its needle points; iron filings show the pattern but not the direction. (b) Direction of the field = direction a free north pole would move: N to S outside the magnet.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Describe the magnetic field between two north poles placed near each other. (b) Explain why magnetic field lines never cross.
items.answer: (a) Field lines from both poles curve away; there is a neutral point midway where the fields cancel. (b) At any point the field has only one direction; if lines crossed, a compass there would point two ways at once.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: lines repel/curve away; 1 mark: neutral point. (b) 1 mark each.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why magnetic field lines never cross. (b) Explain how iron filings show a magnetic field pattern but do not show its direction.
items.answer: (a) At any point the field has only one direction; if lines crossed, a compass there would point two ways at once. (b) Each filing becomes a tiny induced magnet and lines up with the field, but filings have no marked north end, so the direction is not shown.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. (b) 1 mark each.

items.stem: On a field diagram, point Q has field lines 3 times closer together than point Y. State what this tells you about the field and suggest where each point might be on a bar magnet.
items.answer: The field is stronger where lines are closer; the first point is nearer a pole, the second further away (or near the middle/side).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: closer lines = stronger field; 1 mark: sensible positions.
